title: Starting a Nursing Facility in Washington: Licensing, Costs, and Step-by-Step Guide

Introduction (2-3 paragraphs)

Starting a Nursing Facility in Washington represents a meaningful opportunity to serve elderly and disabled individuals requiring institutional care while building a compliant, sustainable care business. Oversight and funding are administered by the Washington State Department of Health (DOH), Health Systems Quality Assurance (HSQA) Division, with reimbursement and program funding for Medicaid coordinated through the Washington State Department of Social and Health Services (DSHS) and its network of Managed Care Organizations (MCOs).

With a significant state market signal—an allocated budget of approximately $1.8 billion for nursing facility services for fiscal years 2024-2025—and robust reimbursement rates between $300-$400 per patient per day, Washington offers a well-funded market for providers prepared to navigate its rigorous licensing, staffing, and compliance requirements. Success hinges on understanding both state regulations and federal mandates to deliver high-quality, person-centered care.

This guide walks you through every step of launching a Nursing Facility in Washington, from understanding complex regulations and licensing procedures to staffing your facility, managing finances, and preparing for state and federal inspections. Whether you are acquiring an existing facility or building a new one, this comprehensive overview will provide the roadmap you need.

Table of Contents

  • Understand Washington’s Nursing Facility Regulations
  • Choose the Type and Size of Your Program
  • Business Structure and Licensing
  • Develop a Comprehensive Business Plan
  • Secure a Suitable Facility or Office
  • Hire and Train Qualified Staff
  • Policies, Procedures, and Care Plans
  • Marketing and Referral Development
  • Maintain Compliance and Prepare for Reviews
  • Frequently Asked Questions

Section 1: Understand Washington’s Nursing Facility Regulations

Washington regulates Nursing Facilities through the Washington State Department of Health (DOH), Health Systems Quality Assurance (HSQA) Division, which is responsible for overseeing licensing, inspections, and compliance with state and federal regulations for nursing facilities. Because most facilities serve residents covered by Medicare or Medicaid, providers must also comply with extensive federal frameworks, including the Centers for Medicare & Medicaid Services (CMS) Conditions of Participation (CoPs) found in 42 CFR Part 483, HIPAA, and the terms of Washington’s 1915(c) waivers like Basic Plus and COPES.

The regulatory framework emphasizes compliance with federal standards, patient safety, quality of care, and staff competency. This includes detailed requirements for resident rights, comprehensive assessments and care planning, quality assurance, infection control, and emergency preparedness. Licenses typically require renewal annually or as determined by the DOH, contingent upon a successful survey and continued compliance. Navigating these Washington nursing facility regulations is the first and most critical step toward opening your doors.

Section 2: Choose the Type and Size of Your Program

Before diving into the licensing process, it’s crucial to define the specific services and scale of your operation. Washington supports multiple Nursing Facility variants, each with different strategic advantages, staffing needs, and reimbursement models:

  • Standard Skilled Nursing Facility: Provides 24/7 skilled nursing, personal care, and rehabilitative services for long-term residents.
  • Specialized Memory Care Units: Features dedicated, secured wings or units designed for the unique safety and cognitive needs of residents with Alzheimer’s disease and other forms of dementia.
  • Short-Term Rehabilitation Services: Focuses on post-acute care for patients recovering from surgery, illness, or injury, with an emphasis on physical, occupational, and speech therapies to facilitate a return to the community.
  • Facilities with Swing Beds: Typically located in Critical Access Hospitals, these beds can ‘swing’ or alternate between providing acute hospital care and post-acute skilled nursing care, offering flexibility in rural areas.

Program size typically ranges from small, 20-bed facilities in rural areas to large, 100+ bed centers in urban hubs. Market analysis shows that demand is strongest and most concentrated in Seattle, Tacoma, and Spokane. In contrast, many rural regions of Washington experience provider shortages, which may offer significant entry opportunities with less direct competition for new providers who can meet the community’s needs.

Section 3: Business Structure and Licensing

Establishing the correct legal and business foundation is essential for long-term success and compliance. In Washington, nursing facility providers typically operate as a Limited Liability Company (LLC), S-Corporation, or C-Corporation to protect personal assets and create a formal business entity.

To become a licensed provider, you must complete several key administrative steps:

  • Register your business with the Washington Secretary of State.
  • Obtain an Employer Identification Number (EIN) from the IRS for tax and employment purposes.
  • Secure required insurance coverage, including professional liability, general liability, and workers’ compensation.
  • Submit a comprehensive licensing application to the Washington State Department of Health (DOH), which includes detailed information about your ownership, management, facility, staffing plan, and policies.

Obtaining a Washington nursing facility license is a meticulous process. Licensing timelines generally range from 6 to 18 months, depending heavily on your team’s readiness, the completeness of your application, and the time required for facility construction or renovation and subsequent inspections.

Section 4: Develop a Comprehensive Business Plan

A robust business plan is your blueprint for financial viability. Startup costs for a nursing facility in Washington are substantial, typically ranging from $500,000 to over $5 million. This wide range depends on whether you lease, purchase, or build a new facility, the extent of renovations, and the cost of specialized medical equipment.

Operating expenses are driven primarily by labor. Staffing represents 55-65% of total operating costs, a significant figure that underscores the importance of efficient scheduling and management while meeting the state-mandated 3.4 Hours Per Resident Day (HPRD). Other major expenses include mortgage/rent, utilities, insurance, food, and medical supplies.

Typical reimbursement or revenue ranges in Washington are strong, providing a path to profitability:

  • Medicaid (Apple Health): $300 – $400 per patient per day, with rates adjusted based on the case-mix of resident acuity.
  • Average Swing Bed Rate: Approximately $357.36 per day (as of July 2025).
  • Medicare: Reimbursement for short-term, post-acute care, often at higher rates than Medicaid.
  • Private Pay: Rates are set by the facility and are typically the highest, often ranging from $400-$600+ per day.

With diligent management and a focus on quality care that attracts referrals, providers operating at a target occupancy of 85% or higher can generally achieve 10-15% gross margins. Your business plan must project a realistic timeline to reach this occupancy level and achieve break-even, which often takes 12-18 months.

Section 5: Secure a Suitable Facility or Office

Your physical facility is the cornerstone of your service and must meet stringent state and federal standards. The building itself is subject to inspection and must be designed for the safety, comfort, and dignity of residents. Key facility requirements, largely derived from federal regulations (42 CFR Part 483) and state building codes, include:

  • Compliance with Americans with Disabilities Act (ADA) accessibility standards throughout the building.
  • Resident rooms that meet specific square footage, privacy, and bathroom accessibility requirements.
  • A commercial-grade kitchen and dining facilities capable of meeting the nutritional needs of all residents.
  • Properly equipped nurse stations with secure medication storage and preparation areas.
  • Comprehensive fire safety systems, including sprinklers, smoke detectors, and alarms that comply with the Life Safety Code.
  • Emergency power systems (generators) to maintain life-support systems, lighting, and critical functions during an outage.

When selecting a location, consider local zoning laws, accessibility for residents’ families and staff, proximity to referral sources like hospitals, and the availability of a qualified local workforce. The right location can significantly impact your ability to maintain census and attract top talent.

Section 6: Hire and Train Qualified Staff

High-quality care is delivered by a high-quality team. Washington’s regulations set specific requirements for key personnel and overall staffing levels. Required roles in a nursing facility typically include:

  • Licensed Nursing Home Administrator (NHA): The overall leader of the facility, who must hold a bachelor’s degree and a valid Washington NHA license.
  • Director of Nursing (DON): A Registered Nurse (RN) with proven leadership experience responsible for overseeing all clinical care.
  • Registered Nurses (RNs) and Licensed Practical Nurses (LPNs): To provide skilled nursing care, administer medications, and supervise direct care staff.
  • Certified Nursing Assistants (CNAs): The frontline caregivers who assist residents with activities of daily living.
  • Support Staff: Including an Activities Director, Social Worker, Registered Dietitian, and housekeeping/maintenance personnel.

Training requirements are strict. CNAs must complete a minimum of 75 hours of state-approved training before they can work independently. All staff must receive initial and ongoing training in critical areas like resident rights, infection control, dementia care, abuse prevention, and emergency procedures. Critically, facilities must meet a minimum staffing level of 3.4 Hours Per Resident Day (HPRD), a key metric regulators will check during surveys.

Section 7: Policies, Procedures, and Care Plans

Operational excellence and regulatory compliance are built on a foundation of comprehensive, well-documented policies and procedures. The DOH and CMS require written policies covering every aspect of facility operation. These are not just for licensing—they are the day-to-day guides for your staff.

Washington requires written policies covering, at a minimum:

  • Resident Rights and Grievance Procedures: Ensuring residents are treated with dignity and have a formal process for voicing concerns.
  • Admission, Transfer, and Discharge Policies: Defining the criteria and processes for resident transitions.
  • Comprehensive Care Planning and Assessment (RAI/MDS): Outlining the process for using the Resident Assessment Instrument (RAI) to create individualized care plans.
  • Infection Prevention and Control Program: A detailed plan for preventing and mitigating the spread of infectious diseases, a major focus of all surveys.
  • Quality Assurance and Performance Improvement (QAPI): A data-driven framework for continuously monitoring and improving care outcomes.
  • Staffing and Competency Evaluation: Policies for hiring, training, and ensuring the ongoing competency of all employees.
  • Emergency Preparedness Plan: A comprehensive plan for responding to natural disasters, fires, and other emergencies.

In addition to facility-wide policies, individual care or service plans must be meticulously developed, reviewed, and documented for each resident according to state and federal rules. This person-centered approach is central to modern nursing facility care.

Section 8: Marketing and Referral Development

Unlike many consumer-facing businesses, marketing a nursing facility is less about public advertising and more about building trusted professional relationships. Your census will be filled primarily through referrals from other healthcare entities. Your key referral sources typically include:

  • Hospital discharge planners and case managers who need to place patients requiring post-acute care.
  • Physician offices and specialty clinics whose patients require long-term skilled nursing.
  • Managed Care Organizations (MCOs) that manage the care and placement of their Medicaid members.
  • Home health and hospice agencies that may have clients whose needs have escalated beyond what can be provided at home.
  • Community-based partners like social workers, elder care attorneys, and senior placement agents.

Successful providers focus on demonstrating impeccable compliance, clinical excellence, responsiveness, and positive outcome documentation. Your reputation with discharge planners and MCOs is your most valuable marketing asset. A clean survey from the DOH, low rehospitalization rates, and positive family testimonials are far more powerful than any advertisement.

Section 9: Maintain Compliance and Prepare for Reviews

Opening your facility is just the beginning. Ongoing success depends on maintaining a constant state of survey readiness. In Washington, oversight includes unannounced inspections from surveyors from the DOH HSQA Division and, for federally certified facilities, CMS contractors. These surveys are intensive, multi-day events where regulators scrutinize every aspect of your operation.

Inspections are focused on identifying deficiencies, with common findings often related to:

  • Infection control lapses, such as improper hand hygiene or personal protective equipment (PPE) usage.
  • Accident prevention and supervision failures, including falls or unmonitored resident elopement.
  • Medication administration errors or improper storage of medications.
  • Incomplete or inaccurate care planning and resident assessments (MDS).
  • Failure to maintain resident dignity, privacy, and rights.

Continuous quality improvement (CQI) and maintaining audit-ready documentation are not optional—they are essential for survival. Regularly conduct self-audits, address issues proactively through your QAPI program, and ensure your staff is always following your written policies. This discipline will protect your residents, your license, and your business.

Section 10: Frequently Asked Questions

  • How long does it take to open a Nursing Facility in Washington?

Opening a nursing facility in Washington can take 12 to 18 months or longer, factoring in business planning, financing, facility acquisition or construction, and the comprehensive DOH licensing and federal certification process.

  • What licenses are required?

You need a Nursing Facility license from the Washington State Department of Health (DOH). If you plan to accept Medicare or Medicaid, which is standard, you must also achieve federal certification from the Centers for Medicare & Medicaid Services (CMS) by demonstrating compliance with 42 CFR Part 483.

  • What reimbursement is available?

Reimbursement primarily comes from Medicaid Apple Health, managed by DSHS and five MCOs, with case-mix adjusted rates from $300-$400 per day. Medicare provides reimbursement for short-term rehabilitation stays, and private pay from residents who cover their own costs is also a significant revenue source.

Conclusion

Starting a Nursing Facility in Washington is a complex but rewarding venture that addresses a critical societal need. The path requires careful planning, a deep understanding of state and federal regulations, and unwavering operational discipline. Providers who invest in robust compliance systems, hire and train excellent staff, and build strong relationships with referral partners are positioned for long-term success in this well-funded and essential sector of the healthcare landscape.
